t: The English chose and prepared the ground: a sloping hillside with its flanks protected, pits dug in front, dismounted men-at-arms in the centre and longbowmen on the flanks, so that the French had to charge uphill.

Estimates of the French army run from about 72,000 or 120,000 in two chronicles to a modern view of at least twice and perhaps three times the English, and the same sources differ on the English as well, from 7,000 to 15,000.
The English laid siege to Calais, which fell eleven months later and stayed in English hands for two hundred years, and the battle established the longbow as a dominant weapon in Western Europe.
dyk: Each English archer was issued two more quivers on the morning of the battle, making 72 arrows per man, and modern historians suggest that half a million arrows could have been shot.
ev: Philip VI's Great Council takes back the lands Edward III holds in France, which marks the start of the Hundred Years' War
A French army under John, Duke of Normandy, marches on Gascony and besieges Aiguillon
The English land at Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue in Normandy and march south, storming Caen on 26 July
The English reach within 2 miles of Paris, then turn north and cross the Somme at the ford of Blanchetaque
The French attack the English position at Crécy-en-Ponthieu, and the Genoese crossbowmen are driven off by the longbowmen
French cavalry charges are broken until nearly midnight, and Philip leaves the field
French forces still arriving are charged by the English, now mounted, and pursued for miles
Calais falls to the English after a siege of eleven months

f.date: 26 August 1346, with the fighting continuing late into the night and a further clash the next morning
f.place: A sloping hillside at Crécy-en-Ponthieu, with Wadicourt on the English left and Crécy and the River Maye on the right, in Ponthieu in northern France
f.sides: England under King Edward III, with the Prince of Wales and the earls of Northampton, Warwick and Arundel, perhaps 7,000 to 15,000 men by modern estimates; France under King Philip VI, with Charles of Alençon, Rudolph of Lorraine and Louis of Blois, by consensus substantially larger, at least twice and perhaps three times the English by Clifford Rogers's estimate
f.outcome: The English held their position through repeated French attacks and suffered very few losses, while the French lost heavily, among them King John of Bohemia and Count Charles of Alençon. Philip left the field near midnight.
